Q: N*N sized Identity Matrix using Higher Order Functions A:

Every answer here makes me go "this is so weird".

Weirder still, I don't know any alternative that isn't also weird.

But here is an answer that isolates the weirdness into a separate function, which makes me feel a little better.

const make_array = (n,f) => Array.from({length:n}, (_,i) => f(i));  // weird
const identitymatrix = n => make_array(n, irow => 
                              make_array(n, icol =>
                                icol===irow ? 1 : 0));
console.log(identitymatrix(3));

Or, here is another way. Maybe it isn't as weird.

But it's still weird that it requires an advanced javascript feature, given that the goal is conceptually so simple.

I sure don't feel that I can show this to a new javascript user and say "here look how simple and clear javascript is".

function* simple_range_generator(n) { for (let i = 0; i < n; ++i) yield i; };
const identitymatrix = n => [...simple_range_generator(n).map(irow =>
                              [...simple_range_generator(n).map(icol =>
                                icol===irow ? 1 : 0)])];
console.log(identitymatrix(3));

I guess what I'm struggling with is that, if I try to refrain from using advanced javascript features, then I end up back uncomfortably in the thick of the Array API which is just... weird.

By "weird", I mean, roughly, "violates the principle of least astonishment, repeatedly".

Q: Are the Espressif linker directive (`DRAM_ATTR`, etc.) at the declaration or definition of functions and variables? A:

The linker directive must be placed at the definition, i.e. option 2 is correct.

First of all, when one looks at source code of the ESP IDF than one sees that this is the way how Espressif developers themselves do it.

Second, it is also obvious that is has to be that way if one considers how the linker works, how this Macro is defined and what the directive is supposed to do.

The macro expands to a special __attribute((...)) directive plus a counter which is increased everytime the macros are evaluated by the preprocessor. The counter helps the linker script to identify the object and place it at the correct memory position.

However, a header file might be included several time by several sources files which constitute different translation units. If the the directive was put at the declaration this would mean the same object would be declared multiple times with different counter values, but the object only exists at a single memory location.

If the macro is placed at the definition than the macro is only evaluated once for esch object as the object can only be part of a unique translation unit. This also makes sense if one considers what the linker does: the linker places the definition of the object (i.e. the function compiled into machine instructions or the data of a varibale) in memory not the declaration.

Q: Where does the .gitignore file belong? A:

The most common place for .gitignore is in the root directory of your repository, which applies ignore rules project-wide. However, you can also drop a .gitignore inside any subdirectory to limit rules strictly to that folder.

For official guidelines, check out the GitHub documentation on ignoring files.

Q: How to build a robust threadpool in C A:

I found a simple and elegant solution for this:

I added a new member to TaskData, a boolean Keep.

When adding a new task, I have to specify if I want the threadpool to keep the task data around even after the task has finished. Basically, this is a requisite for knowing the result of a task, for waiting for it to finish, etc.

Then, on the WaitForTask function, I simply wait in a cycle for the TaskFinished condition, while checking the TaskStatus for the specified task. Since it will never be deleted on the normal loop, there's no longer that problem.

When the TaskStatus is complete, then I return.

Q: Can a user cause a SyntaxError? A:

You're right that it's usually not possible, though there are technically ways to make it happen. That makes this a poor quiz question, because normally the programmer in this situation should not write code that would make that particular exception possible, and if they followed that advice, wouldn't have any reason to worry about catching it.

In the standard documentation, it says about SyntaxError:

This may occur in an import statement, in a call to the built-in functions compile(), exec(), or eval(), or when reading the initial script ...

Normally there's no good reason for user input to be used with any of these. In fact, involving user input in these could be a serious security flaw. But yes, technically you can write code using this to cause a SyntaxError from user input:

>>> eval(input())
2b
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "<stdin>", line 1, in <module>
  File "<string>", line 1
    2b
    ^
SyntaxError: invalid decimal literal
